summary: Proposes a method for managing how the bits of an IPv6 address block are divided up for subnets or customers. It lets an organization postpone the final choice on how many bits go to each level, which makes later growth easier. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Think of numbering rooms in a building without knowing how many floors there will be. This memo shows a way to hand out the digits so you can decide later and not run out.

questions: how to plan ipv6 address space
how to allocate ipv6 addresses flexibly
what is the centermost bit assignment method
how does rfc 3531 improve on rfc 1219
subtitle: A method for managing IPv6 address space without committing all bits upfront.

tldr.problem: When an organization or ISP allocates IPv6 address blocks, they must decide how many bits to assign at each level, but this initial decision often does not scale well when networks grow.
tldr.mechanism: Keep bits near the boundaries between allocation levels unassigned as long as possible. Assign leftmost bits from the left, rightmost bits from the right, and middle bits from the center outward, so partition boundaries can shift without renumbering.
tldr.outcome: This generalization of RFC 1219 lets organizations delay final decisions on address space partitioning and adapt as growth requirements change, postponing exhaustion of available addresses.

facts.label: Boundary flexibility
facts.value: Can shift forward or backward up to assigned bits

today: RFC 3531 is an Informational document that remains current. It has not been obsoleted, and the allocation method it describes is still applicable to IPv6 address planning.

sections.title: The Problem with Fixed Allocations
sections.content:
IPv6 allows flexible address assignment, but initial allocations often fail to scale. A small network may grow larger than expected, needing more addresses. When this happens, the assignment authority cannot allocate contiguous addresses because other networks got them.

RFC 1219 described an IPv4 allocation scheme that keeps unallocated space between the subnet part (on the left) and the host part (on the right) of an address. This lets network designers change the subnet mask later without renumbering the central bits.

RFC 3531 generalizes this approach to work on any parts of an IP address at any allocation authority level—registries, ISPs, organizations, and others. It applies to both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.eli5: If you run out of room in your address plan, you may not be able to fix it without renumbering everything. This memo shows how to leave space in the middle so you can change your plan later.

sections.title: The Allocation Algorithm
sections.content:
Define an IP address as parts p1, p2, p3, ... pN in order, where boundaries between parts are based on what each assignment authority assigns. Part p1 is typically the leftmost part assigned by a registry. Part p2 might go to a large ISP or national registry. Part p3 to a customer or smaller provider. Each part has a length l(pX).

The algorithm allocates addresses differently in each part:

  • For p1 (leftmost): assign using leftmost bits first
  • For pN (rightmost): assign using rightmost bits first
  • For center parts: assign using center bits first

This keeps unassigned bits near the boundaries between parts. The prefix boundary between any two parts can shift forward or backward later, up to the assigned bits.
sections.eli5: From the left side, hand out numbers starting with the left edge. From the right side, hand out from the right edge. In the middle, hand out from the center. This leaves gaps at the edges so you can move the boundaries.

sections.title: Detailed Assignment Methods
sections.content:
Leftmost assignment uses a mirror of binary counting: 00000000, 10000000, 01000000, 11000000, 00100000, and so on. This assigns bits one at a time from the left edge, creating new combinations as each round adds bits.

Rightmost assignment uses standard binary counting: 00000000, 00000001, 00000010, 00000011, 00000100, and so on. Bits fill from the right edge.

Centermost assignment for middle parts with a predefined length works by selecting the middle bit first (or the bit following center if even), creating all combinations of selected bits, then expanding by adding one more bit per round. Even rounds add the preceding bit; odd rounds add the subsequent bit. For an 8-bit part, the order is 00000000, 00001000, 00010000, 00011000, 00000100, 00001100, 00010100, 00011100, 00100000, and so on.
sections.eli5: Three different counting tricks: left edge counts from left, right edge counts normally, and middle parts count from the center outward to both sides.

sections.title: Example: Multi-Level Address Delegation
sections.content:
Provider P1 holds 3ffe:0b00/24 and allocates to customers. It expects 256 customers (8 bits) and one customer C2 expects 1024 sub-customers (10 more bits).

P1 assigns to its customers using leftmost bits: 10000000 to C1, 01000000 to C2, 11000000 to C3, 00100000 to C4. C2 assigns to its customers using centermost bits: 0000010000 to C2C1, 0000100000 to C2C2, 0000110000 to C2C3. C2C3's full address becomes the P1 prefix (3ffe:0b00:0b00), P1's allocation to C2 (01000000), and C2's allocation to C2C3 (00001100 00).

By this method, P1 can add more customers and C2 can adjust assumptions about sub-customer size until the reserved bits are assigned.
sections.eli5: A provider gives addresses to customers on the left, customers give addresses to sub-customers in the middle, and they both have room to grow by using the unassigned bits at the edges.
